tagline: A creekside orchard and hairpin turns on the climb from Sedona
intro: State Route 89A follows Oak Creek Canyon north from Sedona, climbing approximately 2,200 feet toward the rim. The Forest Service presents this scenic drive as a route of dense tree canopies, red rock views and hairpin turns, with switchbacks at its northern end. It gives the drive as 15 miles and about an hour, on an entirely paved road.

The state completed a road through the canyon in 1914. Frank Pendley had already acquired his homestead and planted an apple orchard, supported by an irrigation system he developed. In 1933 he built tourist cabins, some of which survive at Slide Rock. The apple farm remains one of the canyon’s preserved homesteads, and the irrigation system continues in use.

Heading north from Sedona, the drive enters the canyon from the junction of Routes 179 and 89A. Slide Rock lies seven miles north of town. Oak Creek runs along the canyon floor year-round, one of the high desert region’s few perennial streams. At the northern end, the switchbacks climb to Oak Creek Vista on the rim, on the right for northbound travelers. The rock changes along the canyon: red and pale sandstones dominate southern cliffs, while Kaibab Limestone and the Toroweap Formation appear at the northern end beneath the east rim’s basalt lava flows.
notice: The northern switchbacks carry the road from the canyon floor to the rim.

moments.title: Slide Rock
moments.text: Slide Rock is both a natural water slide and a working apple farm. Frank L. Pendley arrived in the canyon in 1907, acquired title under the Homestead Act in 1910 and planted apples in 1912. His irrigation system remains in use, and some of the tourist cabins he built in 1933 survive. Arizona State Parks purchased the property in 1985, and the park was dedicated in 1987. The 43-acre apple farm sits among tall red rock formations beside the slippery creek bed that gave the park its name. The Pendley Homestead Trail covers a quarter mile within the park.

moments.title: East Pocket Knob
moments.text: The climb toward East Pocket Knob follows a trail first built to reach grazing pastures. C.S. (Bear) Howard laid it out in the 1880s; the Civilian Conservation Corps reconstructed it during the 1930s under A.B. Young’s supervision. The strenuous A. B. Young Trail gains 1,950 feet in two miles one way, negotiating 33 switchbacks to the summit lookout. Built in 1943, the lookout is one of two wooden fire lookouts remaining in Arizona. Dark-gray basalt overlies light-colored Coconino Sandstone on the mountain. The summit stands 2,000 feet above Oak Creek Canyon within a horizontal distance of one mile.

moments.title: Oak Creek Vista
moments.text: Oak Creek Vista stands at the canyon rim above the northern switchbacks. On the drive north from Sedona, the overlook is on the right after the last mile of climbing turns. The canyon’s east rim is formed by basalt lava flows, while Kaibab Limestone and the Toroweap Formation appear only at the northern end. Farther south, the cliffs expose red Schnebly Hill sandstone and buff to white Coconino Sandstone.
